sentence: I bought a used car yesterday. ___ car needs two new tyres.
setupText: Choose the words that keep talking about the same car.
taskText: I bought a used car yesterday. ___ car needs two new tyres.
text: Choose the words that keep talking about the same car. I bought a used car yesterday. ___ car needs two new tyres.
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-381:Maintaining a referent across a short narrative
explanation: "The car" refers back to the used car just introduced. Repeating "a car" would not clearly maintain that reference.

rationales.An: "Car" begins with /k/, so "an car" is incorrect.
rationales.The: The reader already knows which car is being discussed: the one bought yesterday.
rationales.A: This would introduce a car without explicitly linking it to the previous sentence. The task asks you to maintain the same reference.
rationales.(nothing): The singular noun "car" needs a determiner; it cannot start this sentence alone.

sentence: My new position begins tomorrow. The company has sent me ___ about my first day.
taskText: My new position begins tomorrow. The company has sent me ___ about my first day.
text: Choose the grammatically correct phrase. My new position begins tomorrow. The company has sent me ___ about my first day.
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-382:Article with a unit of an uncountable noun
explanation: "Information" is uncountable. To refer to one detail, use the countable phrase "a piece of information".

rationales.an information: English does not normally count information as "an information". Count a piece or an item of information instead.
rationales.a piece of information: "A" introduces the singular countable noun "piece", while "information" stays uncountable.
rationales.an piece of information: "Piece" starts with /p/, so the article must be "a".
rationales.a piece of informations: The uncountable noun stays "information" after "a piece of"; it does not take plural -s.

sentence: Please turn the music down. I've got ___.
setupText: Choose the correct phrase for this feeling.
taskText: Please turn the music down. I've got ___.
text: Choose the correct phrase for this feeling. Please turn the music down. I've got ___.
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-383:A in the fixed expression have a headache
explanation: The usual expression is "have a headache". "Headache" is a singular countable noun and begins with a pronounced /h/.

rationales.headache: This expression normally needs an article: "I've got a headache".
rationales.an headache: The /h/ in "headache" is pronounced, so use "a".
rationales.a headache: "A headache" correctly names one instance of this discomfort.
rationales.a headaches: "A" cannot introduce the plural "headaches". Use singular "headache" here.

sentence: Which sentence uses the day name correctly?
setupText: Choose the sentence about a regular weekly class.
taskText: Which sentence uses the day name correctly?
text: Choose the sentence about a regular weekly class. Which sentence uses the day name correctly?
options: We have training every the Monday.
We have training on a Mondays.
We have training on an Mondays.
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-384:No article with plural weekday names for routines
explanation: "On Mondays" means regularly on that day of the week. The plural day name does not take an article in this expression.

Do not combine "every" with "the" here. You can say "every Monday".
The singular article "a" cannot introduce the plural day name "Mondays".
"An" is singular and does not match either the plural form or the initial consonant sound.
The plural day name without an article expresses the repeated weekly event.

sentence: This isn't a language school. It's ___.
taskText: This isn't a language school. It's ___.
text: Choose the grammatically correct phrase. This isn't a language school. It's ___.
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-385:A before a written vowel with a consonant sound
explanation: "University" starts with the consonant sound /y/, as in "you". The spelling starts with u, but the sound requires "a".

rationales.an university: The initial sound is /y/, not a vowel sound. Write "a university".
rationales.a university: "A" agrees with the initial sound and introduces one institution of this kind.
rationales.university: When classifying this institution after "It is", the singular noun needs a determiner.
rationales.a universities: "A" means one; it cannot be followed by the plural "universities".

sentence: At the tourist office: 'We're looking for ___ near the beach.'
setupText: No hotel has been mentioned. Choose the phrase for one hotel of the kind wanted, not a particular hotel or an extra one.
taskText: At the tourist office: 'We're looking for ___ near the beach.'
text: No hotel has been mentioned. Choose the phrase for one hotel of the kind wanted, not a particular hotel or an extra one. At the tourist office: 'We're looking for ___ near the beach.'
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-386:Indefinite reference to something sought but not yet selected
explanation: A small hotel describes one place of the kind the travellers want. They can use a before they have found or chosen that place.

rationales.the small hotel: The suggests that the listener can identify which hotel is meant. The travellers are introducing the kind they want.
rationales.another small hotel: Another asks for a different or additional hotel. That adds a comparison with a hotel not mentioned in this request.
rationales.a small hotel: This introduces one hotel of the desired kind without identifying it in advance.
rationales.that small hotel: That points to a particular hotel, perhaps one already discussed. No such hotel has been identified here.

sentence: Flights are expensive, so we're going to Paris ___.
setupText: Choose the usual phrase naming the means of travel.
taskText: Flights are expensive, so we're going to Paris ___.
text: Choose the usual phrase naming the means of travel. Flights are expensive, so we're going to Paris ___.
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-387:Zero article when naming a transport method with by
explanation: Use "by train" to name the means of travel. In this expression, "by" is followed by the transport word without an article.

rationales.by train: This names the travel method using the standard by + transport expression.
rationales.by a train: A train counts one vehicle. The usual expression naming this means of travel is by train, without an article.
rationales.by an train: An cannot come before the consonant sound at the start of train. The method expression also needs no article.
rationales.by the train: The train identifies a particular vehicle. That can occur in other contexts, but the ordinary phrase for the travel method alone is by train.

sentence: The repair took exactly sixty minutes: ___.
taskText: The repair took exactly sixty minutes: ___.
text: Choose the grammatically correct phrase. The repair took exactly sixty minutes: ___.
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-388:An before silent h in hour
explanation: "Hour" begins with a vowel sound because its h is silent. One period of sixty minutes is "an hour".

rationales.a hour: The first spoken sound in "hour" is a vowel, so "a" must become "an".
rationales.an hour: The article follows the sound, not the silent written h.
rationales.hour: To name one countable period here, include the article: "an hour".

sentence: Check ___ before you travel.
setupText: Choose the phrase for all the details printed on this ticket.
taskText: Check ___ before you travel.
text: Choose the phrase for all the details printed on this ticket. Check ___ before you travel.
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-389:The with identified uncountable information
explanation: "On your ticket" identifies the information to check. Although "information" is uncountable, it can take "the" when it refers to specific details.

rationales.an information on your ticket: "Information" is uncountable; "an information" is not a standard singular unit.
rationales.a information on your ticket: The uncountable noun does not take "a", and the following sound is a vowel as well.
rationales.the information on your ticket: "The" identifies the particular set of details printed on the ticket.
rationales.the informations on your ticket: "Information" does not normally have a plural -s form in English.

sentence: My sister lives in ___ United States.
setupText: Choose the words for this country name.
taskText: My sister lives in ___ United States.
text: Choose the words for this country name. My sister lives in ___ United States.
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-390:The in the established name the United States
explanation: The conventional country name is "the United States". Some multiword country names use "the", even though names such as Japan do not.

rationales.a: "A United States" does not name the country in this ordinary location sentence.
rationales.an: The name does not take "an"; "United" also starts with a consonant sound.
rationales.(nothing): The country name normally includes "the" in a full sentence: "in the United States".
rationales.the: "The United States" is the established form of this country name.

sentence: The map has bus routes and opening times. What ___!
taskText: The map has bus routes and opening times. What ___!
text: Choose the grammatically correct phrase. The map has bus routes and opening times. What ___!
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-391:Article in a what exclamation with a singular noun
explanation: The exclamation is "What a useful guide!". "Useful" begins with the consonant sound /y/, so it takes "a".

rationales.an useful guide: The written u in "useful" represents a /y/ sound at the start. Use "a".
rationales.useful guide: A singular countable noun in this exclamation needs an article: "What a useful guide!".
rationales.a useful guide: This puts "a" before the adjective and uses the correct sound-based choice.
rationales.a useful guides: "A" cannot introduce the plural "guides" in this exclamation.

sentence: At the cafe: "Two coffees, please: ___ and a cappuccino."
taskText: At the cafe: "Two coffees, please: ___ and a cappuccino."
text: Choose the grammatically correct phrase. At the cafe: "Two coffees, please: ___ and a cappuccino."
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-392:An with a drink interpreted as one serving
explanation: A drink name can be countable when it means one serving. "An espresso" is one serving, and "espresso" begins with a vowel sound.

rationales.a espresso: For this vowel sound, the singular article is "an".
rationales.an espresso: This correctly names one serving of espresso within the two-drink order.
rationales.a espressos: "A" cannot introduce plural "espressos" and does not match the initial vowel sound.

sentence: Both bags look blue to me. Are they ___ colour?
taskText: Both bags look blue to me. Are they ___ colour?
text: Choose the grammatically correct phrase. Both bags look blue to me. Are they ___ colour?
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-393:The in the expression the same
explanation: The normal expression is "the same colour". English uses "the" with "same" in this comparison.

rationales.a same: Do not use "a same" in this expression; say "the same".
rationales.an same: "An same" is not the expression and also mismatches the /s/ sound.
rationales.same: In this full question, include "the": "Are they the same colour?".
rationales.the same: "The same colour" asks whether the colours match.

sentence: After work, we usually play ___ with our neighbours.
setupText: Choose the ordinary way to name the sport.
taskText: After work, we usually play ___ with our neighbours.
text: Choose the ordinary way to name the sport. After work, we usually play ___ with our neighbours.
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-394:Zero article with a sport after play
explanation: Sport names normally have no article after "play": "play tennis". The sentence names an activity, not one countable match.

rationales.tennis: "Play tennis" is the standard phrase for taking part in this sport.
rationales.a tennis: "Tennis" does not count a single match. You could say "a game of tennis".
rationales.an tennis: "An" neither fits the initial consonant sound nor belongs before this sport name here.
rationales.the tennis: The usual activity phrase is "play tennis". "The tennis" can refer to a particular competition in other constructions.

sentence: We usually eat toast, but yesterday the hotel served us ___.
taskText: We usually eat toast, but yesterday the hotel served us ___.
text: Choose the grammatically correct phrase. We usually eat toast, but yesterday the hotel served us ___.
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-395:A with a described instance of a meal
explanation: An ordinary meal name can become countable when we describe one particular meal: "a big breakfast".

rationales.an big breakfast: "Big" begins with /b/, so the article is "a".
rationales.big breakfast: The phrase describes one meal with an adjective; it needs a determiner such as "a" here.
rationales.a big breakfast: "A" introduces one breakfast described as big, rather than the routine activity of eating breakfast.
rationales.a big breakfasts: "A" introduces one meal and cannot be followed by plural "breakfasts".

sentence: At reception, please show ___ with a photo.
taskText: At reception, please show ___ with a photo.
text: Choose the grammatically correct phrase. At reception, please show ___ with a photo.
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-396:An before an initialism pronounced with a vowel sound
explanation: The letter I is pronounced with a vowel sound. Because ID is read as letter names, the phrase is "an ID card".

rationales.a ID card: Use the sound of the letter name I. It begins with a vowel sound and needs "an".
rationales.an ID card: "An" matches the spoken beginning of ID and introduces one card.
rationales.an ID cards: The article is singular, so the noun must be "card", not "cards".
rationales.ID card: The singular countable phrase needs a determiner in this request.

sentence: We saw three flats at different prices. We chose ___.
setupText: Choose the phrase that identifies the lowest-priced flat out of all three.
taskText: We saw three flats at different prices. We chose ___.
text: Choose the phrase that identifies the lowest-priced flat out of all three. We saw three flats at different prices. We chose ___.
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-397:Definite superlative identifying the lowest-priced member of a stated group
explanation: The cheapest flat identifies the one with the lowest price in the group of three. A cheap flat only says that its price is low; it does not rank it against the other two.

rationales.a cheap flat: This describes a flat as low-priced. It does not say it costs less than both of the others.
rationales.another cheap flat: Another introduces a different or additional low-priced flat, not the lowest-priced one in the stated group.
rationales.the cheaper flat: Cheaper makes a comparison, normally between two alternatives. It does not explicitly identify the lowest price out of all three as cheapest does.
rationales.the cheapest flat: The + cheapest + flat identifies the lowest-priced member of this group.

sentence: Which sentence is correct?
taskText: Which sentence is correct?
text: Choose the grammatically correct sentence. Which sentence is correct?
options: My brother gave me an useful advice.
My brother gave me a useful advice.
My brother gave me some useful advice.
My brother gave me some useful advices.
answer: My brother gave me some useful advice.
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-398:Some rather than a or an with modified advice
explanation: "Advice" is uncountable, so "some useful advice" works without a or an. An adjective does not make advice countable.

"Some" can introduce an unspecified amount of the uncountable noun "advice".
"Advice" cannot be introduced by "an" here, and "useful" begins with a consonant sound.
An adjective does not turn "advice" into a singular countable noun. Say "some useful advice" or "a useful piece of advice".
The noun remains "advice", without plural -s, in standard English.

sentence: I take this medicine twice ___: once in the morning and once at night.
taskText: I take this medicine twice ___: once in the morning and once at night.
text: Choose the grammatically correct phrase. I take this medicine twice ___: once in the morning and once at night.
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-399:A expressing frequency per unit of time
explanation: "Twice a day" means two times each day. Here "a" expresses a repeated rate, not an unidentified calendar day.

rationales.an day: "Day" begins with /d/, so it cannot follow "an".
rationales.a day: "A day" expresses the daily frequency and matches the two times specified.
rationales.a days: The article "a" takes the singular unit "day", not plural "days".
rationales.day: The frequency expression requires "a day" or "per day" after "twice".

sentence: The shop assistant offers two sizes: 'Would you like ___?'
taskText: The shop assistant offers two sizes: 'Would you like ___?'
text: Choose the grammatically correct phrase. The shop assistant offers two sizes: 'Would you like ___?'
options: an small or an large bag
a small or a large bags
a small or a large bag
answer: a small or a large bag
focusKey: coverage-articles-a2-400:Articles in coordinated alternatives sharing a noun
explanation: A small or a large bag offers two possible sizes of one bag. Repeating a before large is correct; a small or large bag, with one shared article, is also possible.

rationales.small or large bag: The singular noun "bag" needs a determiner in this full question, even when two adjectives are offered.
rationales.an small or an large bag: Both "small" and "large" begin with consonant sounds, so neither can follow "an".
rationales.a small or a large bag: Both alternatives correctly introduce a possible singular bag with "a".
rationales.a small or a large bags: The article "a" cannot introduce the plural noun "bags".
